mission_1.search: On the open map, the BFS path length is 13.5 and the expanded-node count is 928. On the open map, the A* path length is 13.5 and the expanded-node count is 700. The lengths are equal for both of them, but A* examined fewer cells. The queue produced this result of 928 for BFS by starting at the starting cell and then adding all its reachable neighbors to the queue. The neighboring nodes for each cell is added until the goal is reached or ever cell is marked visited and the queue is then empty. Since the queue is FIFO, the neighbors from the previous cell are visited in order one depth at a time with its neighboring children cells all being added to the end of the queue. Since the depths are expanded one at a time, it examines more cells. The heuristic produced this result of 700 for A* by calculating the manhattan distance and adding it to the current cost to reach the current cell + 1 in order to determine the priority for the current cell's neighboring cells and updating that cost if a smaller cost to that cell was found. Since the open map is a unit-cost grid, the queue and heuristic produced this result of equal path lengths because the queue for BFS always finds the shortest number of edges by expanding one depth at a time and since the heuristic uses manhattan distance, it doesn't overestimate the remaining cost for a cell so it also finds the shortest number path which is equal to the queue in BFS.
mission_1.failure: On the constrained map, the DFS and IDDFS expanded-node counts are 524 and 25001, respectively and the path lengths are 104 and 0, respectively since IDDFS reached its resource limit with 250001 expansions so it wasn't able to determine a path even if there is one. On the constrained map, the BFS expanded-node count is 848 and the path length is 24.5. BFS and DFS have the same status of completed while IDDFS has the status resource limit. One difference in expansions is that the expanded-node count for BFS at 848 is way smaller than the expanded-node count for IDDFS at 250001, reaching a resource limit because BFS uses the queue to expand one depth at a time until the goal is reached if possible, starting from the starting cell, processing all the current neighboring cells before processing children cells of those neighboring cells, and continuing to do that since the queue is FIFO which results in the shortest path length in the unit-cost grid and thus also less expansions. However, IDDFS expands as far as possible in one path with an increasing depth of expansion which caused it to continue to go and expand down one path for all its starting cell's neighboring cells and their neighboring children cells to try to reach the goal for multiple depth limits until it reached the goal or hit the current depth limit which resulted in so many expansions that it led to a resource limit with 250001 expansions. DFS had a smaller expanded-node count than BFS at 524 because it searches all the connected cells starting from the starting cell's neighboring cells until it reaches the goal or has no more cells to expand to in which it goes back to the last previous cell with more expansions since the stack is LIFO which causes DFS to use the first path that reaches the goal by expanding as far as possible in one path which resulted in DFS getting lucky and expanding on this path to the goal quickly for the constrained map which led to the smaller expanded-node count at 524. All four unreachable-case statuses are no_path for all the search algorithms. The difference between no_path and resource_limit is that no_path means that there is no path to go from the starting cell to goal cell meaning that the goal cell is unreachable from the starting cell, but resource_limit means that the test runner simply ran out of expansions or time while searching for a path from the starting cell to goal cell and doesn't necessarily mean that there exists no path from the starting cell to the goal. I also checked whether the results from all the tests made sense for all the algorithms like if BFS and A* produced the same shortest path length for the unit-cost grids.
